meta.title: Who really said "He that can have patience can have what he will"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Benjamin Franklin printed this maxim in Poor Richard's Almanack, June 1736. The popular "He who can have patience" wording is a later drift.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He that can have patience can have what he will'?
meta.ogDescription: Franklin printed it in Poor Richard's Almanack for 1736 — but by his own account he gleaned most of Poor Richard's proverbs from older books.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Franklin printed this as a calendar maxim in Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1736 — the Yale Papers of Benjamin Franklin text at Founders Online ↗ carries it on the June calendar page. The wording he set in type was “He that can have Patience, can have what he will”; the widely circulated “He who…” version is a later drift.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Calendar maxim on the June page (“IV Mon. June hath xxx days”)
“He that can have Patience, can have what he will.”

source.excerpt:
He that buys by the penny, maintains not only himself, but other people.
He that can have Patience, can have what he will.
Now I’ve a sheep and a cow, every body bids me good morrow.
trail: The almanac itself, as edited in the Yale Papers of Benjamin Franklin and published in full at Founders Online ↗, carries the line on the June calendar page — under the heading “IV Mon. June hath xxx days”, just after “He that buys by the penny…” closes May.
Wikiquote’s year-by-year list of Poor Richard maxims ↗ places “He that can have Patience, can have what he will” among the 1736 entries.
Wikiquote’s Patience page ↗ narrows it further, citing Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard’s Almanack, June 1736.

A 1914 public-domain selection of Franklin’s sayings, digitised by the Internet Archive ↗, carries the line at numbered entry 210 — modernised to “He that can have patience can have what he will.”, without the 1736 capital and comma. It is alphabetised and undated, so it witnesses the saying, not the 1736 page.
On how much of Poor Richard was Franklin’s own, Wikipedia quotes Jill Lepore ↗: he wrote perhaps one proverb in ten and found the rest in books, especially Thomas Fuller’s 1732 Gnomologia.
source.excerptNote: Three maxims as they run in the 1736 almanac: the first closes the May calendar page, the next two open June’s. Poor Richard’s sayings were set one to a line in the narrow margins of the calendar, so there is no surrounding paragraph — the neighbours are the context.

source.rightsNote: Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1736 was printed and sold in Philadelphia in the closing months of 1735 — almanacs went on sale the year before the one they covered — and the reprint cited alongside it appeared in 1914. Both are far earlier than the 1931 US public-domain cutoff. The text is free to quote, reproduce and adapt without permission.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: Who was Benjamin Franklin?
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was a Philadelphia printer who became one of the most consequential Americans of his century — scientist, diplomat, and signer of the Declaration of Independence. From 1732 to 1758 he wrote, compiled and printed Poor Richard’s Almanack under the pen name Richard Saunders, filling its calendar margins with the terse maxims that made him the most quoted American of the age. He was candid that the wisdom was not all his: by his own reckoning he wrote perhaps one proverb in ten, and gleaned the rest from earlier books.

cite.sourceCitation: Franklin, Benjamin [as “Richard Saunders”]. Poor Richard, 1736: An Almanack for the Year of Christ 1736. Philadelphia: printed and sold by B. Franklin, maxim on the June page. Text as edited in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, ed. Leonard W. Labaree, vol. 2 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1961), pp. 136–145; online at Founders Online. The line also appears, modernised and undated, in Poor Richard’s Almanack: Selections from the Apothegms and Proverbs (Waterloo, IA: The U.S.C. Publishing Co., 1914), no. 210.

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Franklin holds up — the line really is in his almanac. Two smaller things go astray anyway: the wording, and the assumption that printing a proverb is the same as inventing one.

items.why: Franklin set “He that can have Patience, can have what he will.” The who variant is the one that spread through user-submitted quote sites — Goodreads carries it with no source at all ↗, under a notice that its quotes are community-added and unverified.

Even the aggregators that get the wording right usually strip the provenance: BrainyQuote prints the correct “He that” text ↗ with Franklin’s life dates but names no work and no year, leaving nothing a reader can check.

Printing it in 1736 does not mean he coined it. Franklin admitted “not a tenth Part of the Wisdom was my own” ↗, and Wikipedia quotes Jill Lepore to the effect that he took most of Poor Richard’s proverbs from anthologies such as Thomas Fuller’s 1732 Gnomologia ↗. No earlier printed source for this particular line turned up in the sources consulted here.

misattribution.truthLine: Documented: Benjamin Franklin printed “He that can have Patience, can have what he will” in Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1736 ↗. Undocumented: that he was the first to say it.

context.heading: Why a one-line proverb was worth printing
lead: Poor Richard’s Almanack was not a quote book. It was a working calendar — moon phases, tide tables, weather guesses — and Franklin used the blank slivers beside the dates to slip in maxims. A line had to earn its place by being short enough to fit and sharp enough to be remembered, which is why so much of Franklin’s reputation as a sage rests on sentences of a dozen words. This is one of them: patience reframed not as endurance but as leverage.

The almanac ran for a quarter-century — issues for 1733 through 1758 — and sold as many as 10,000 copies a year across the colonies. That reach is why a passing proverb from a 1736 calendar page is still printed on posters today — and also why its authorship gets flattened. Anything Poor Richard said, Franklin gets credited with.
detailsBody: In the preface to the final almanac — the piece later famous as The Way to Wealth — Franklin has Poor Richard listen to an old man quoting him back at himself, and admits that “not a tenth Part of the Wisdom was my own which he ascribed to me” ↗. Historians take him at his word: Wikipedia quotes Jill Lepore noting that Franklin found most of the proverbs in anthologies, especially Thomas Fuller’s 1732 Gnomologia ↗, and that his real gift was compression — turning Fuller’s “A Man in Passion rides a horse that runs away with him” into “A Man in a Passion rides a mad Horse.”

For this particular maxim, none of the sources consulted here documents an earlier printed appearance. That is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence: given Franklin’s habits, an older English proverb behind it would be no surprise — but no one has produced one.
